The Republic of South Sudan (RSS) became an independent nation on July 9, 2011, following decades of civil war. Two years following independence, the country was plunged into a state of prolonged insecurity and economic challenges following internal political crisis in December 2013 and in July 2016. A peace agreement was signed in 2018 and a transitional government was formed in early 2020. This situation adversely affected the national health system and access to health services by the population. The health infrastructure is limited, the health system is understaffed due to variety of factors including the high attrition rate, inability of the government to pay health sector salaries on a regular basis, with several months in salary payments outstanding. The political and economic instability has resulted in persistent low national budgetary allocation to the health sector. These country context challenges have negative effects on population health, particularly vulnerability to epidemic diseases such as HIV, TB and malaria and on efforts to address and respond to these challenges. As a result, the Ministry of Health receives significant support from Humanitarian and Development partners to undertake its mandate. This situation is likely to continue in the foreseeable future. The Service Availability and Readiness Assessment (SARA) survey conducted in 2018 highlighted key gaps in health system performance and service delivery. According to the survey, the General and Specific Service Availability and Readiness Scores for most of the indicators were far below the WHO recommended minimum thresholds . South Sudan continues to be classified under the Global Fund as a challenging operating environment (COE) country, having the characteristics of both protracted emergency and chronic instability according to this definition. Therefore, the country shall continue to be supported by the GF. Like other countries, the situation with response to COVID-19 pandemic has evolved. The focus is shifting to strengthening systems for health and pandemic preparedness, while continuing to implement measures to prevent the spread of the disease. COVID-19 response had significant knock-on effects on HIV, Tuberculosis (TB) and malaria programs, as such mitigation of the effects and putting in place recovery measures also remains a priority for the country. Effective and timely response to current and future pandemic necessitates that the country strengthens its system for health. Therefore, the country welcomes the GF Board decision on C19RM funding remaining flexible so that as COVID-19 evolves, resources can be directed to emerging priority areas including “towards longer-term investments in health systems’ infrastructure and capacities for pandemic preparedness and response”. South Sudan shall leverage on the GF fund to continue building its system for health so that its resilient and in position to effectively respond to pandemics while providing routine services including programs for Malaria, TB and HIV/AIDS. The COVID-19 Response Mechanism (C10RM) grant continues to contribute to the robust response by South Sudan to COVID-19 pandemic. The investment so far has also helped in mitigating the risk posed by COVID-19 on HIV/TB/Malaria programmes. While the Global Fund resources have so far been instrumental in the response to COVID-19 pandemic, there remain critical gaps in both COVID-19 response and in pandemic preparedness and response by the country.

title.narrative: The project integrates climate risks in programming

description.narrative: The integration of climate risks in programming includes an undertaking of concrete actions to reduce and/or mitigate risks related to climate change impact and disaster risks ( for example droughts, erosion, salinization, flooding, etc.) The projects we refer to could be on the themes of health education, justice, security, disaster management, finance and livelihoods.
